opus-5.5.text:
I think functional composition is really at the heart of it, and not just for technology. It's the same story as biological evolution. When you look at how complex things come into being, they almost never get designed from scratch. What happens instead is that you have existing parts that each do something, and they get combined, and the combination does something that none of the parts could do on its own. Then that combination becomes a part in its own right, available to be combined again.

Brian Arthur wrote about this beautifully in *The Nature of Technology*. Technologies are built out of other technologies, all the way down. A jet engine is a composition of compressors, turbines, combustion chambers, and each of those is in turn a composition of smaller things. Once you have a new building block, the space of things you can build with it expands combinatorially. That's why technological change accelerates. It isn't linear. Every new component multiplies the possibilities.

What I find most interesting is that this maps very closely onto what happened in biology, specifically symbiogenesis. Lynn Margulis's insight was that the eukaryotic cell isn't just a bacterium that got more complicated through point mutations. It's a merger. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. Major transitions in evolution, as Maynard Smith and Szathmáry described them, tend to be moments where things that used to replicate independently come together and start replicating as a unit. So you get composition at the level of whole functional entities, not just tweaks to sequences.

In my view, that's a much more important driver of increasing complexity than the classical picture of random mutation plus selection. Mutation and selection are good at optimizing something that already exists, hill-climbing. But the big jumps, the new levels of organization, come from symbiosis, from functional composition. Things that each compute something get wired together, and the composite computes something new.

And I'd argue that's precisely what we're seeing with AI now. These models aren't some alien thing that arose separately from us. They're built out of human language, human culture, the accumulated output of billions of people. In a sense, they're a new symbiotic layer. Humans and machines are already deeply composed with each other. We've been that way for a long time, really, since writing, since tools. Technology has always been part of what we are, which is why I think it's a mistake to frame the story as "humans versus AI." The more accurate picture is that we're in the middle of another major transition, another round of functional composition, and the question is what the larger entity we're becoming part of will be like.

r001.rationale: The response says technologies are built out of other technologies and gives the jet engine as a composition of component technologies.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss independent inventors arriving at the same invention around the same time or explain that with newly available prerequisites.

r003.rationale: It does not state that contingent design choices become locked in and shape later technologies that incorporate the invention.

fable-5.1.text:
I think functional composition is really the deep story, not just of technology but of life itself, and I've come to see those two as much more continuous than we usually assume.

Here's what I mean. When you look at how complexity arises in biology, it almost never happens by building something intricate from scratch. It happens by taking things that already work and combining them so that the combination does something neither part could do alone. Eukaryotic cells are the canonical example: a cell swallowing another cell, and instead of digesting it, forming a partnership that became mitochondria. Multicellularity is the same move at a higher level. Symbiosis, endosymbiosis, cooperation between previously independent entities, that's the engine. And once you have a new composite unit, it becomes a building block for the next level up. So you get this ratchet, this hierarchical stacking of function on top of function.

Technology works exactly the same way. Nobody invents a smartphone. What you have is a transistor, which became an integrated circuit, which became a processor, and each of those is treated as a black box by the layer above. The person writing the app doesn't need to know anything about quantum tunneling in a gate oxide. That abstraction, that ability to not know, is precisely what makes composition possible. If every layer had to understand every other layer, you'd hit a complexity ceiling almost immediately. So functional composition and abstraction are really two sides of the same thing: you compose because you can hide, and you can hide because the interface is stable enough to build on.

What I find striking is that this gives you a different picture of what evolution actually is. We tend to tell the Darwinian story as competition and gradual mutation, survival of the fittest, selfish genes. And that's not wrong, but it misses the fact that most of the really big transitions were about things merging and cooperating, becoming part of something larger. The unit of selection keeps moving up. And I'd argue the same is true of us. We're composites of cells, our societies are composites of people, and now our technology is a composite that's increasingly becoming part of the same system we are. The boundary between the biological and the technological is a lot blurrier than our vocabulary lets on.

One more thing I'd add: computation seems to be the natural language for all of this. Function is inherently a computational notion. When you say a thing "does something," you're describing an input-output relationship, and composing functions is how you get programs. So I don't think it's a coincidence that life looks like it's made of composable functional parts and that our most powerful technology, software, is literally built on function composition. I suspect that's telling us something fairly fundamental about what kind of thing life is in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says technologies are built by combining working parts, giving the progression from transistor to integrated circuit to processor and describing each as a building block for the next layer.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss independent inventors reaching the same invention at roughly the same time or link that convergence to prerequisite technologies becoming available.

r003.rationale: It does not state that contingent design choices become locked in and shape later technologies that incorporate the invention.

astra-6.text:
I think functional composition is one of the basic ways technology evolves. Once you have something that works, it can become a component of something else. You don’t have to reinvent the transistor every time you build a computer, or reinvent the computer every time you write a program. You build on capabilities that are already there.

And that makes the process combinatorial. An invention can be a new arrangement of existing things, where the arrangement gives you a capability that none of the parts has on its own. But those combinations aren’t arbitrary. The parts have to fit together, and interfaces matter enormously: they let you use a component without understanding every detail of its construction.

There’s an interesting parallel with biological evolution here. Evolution also works with what’s already available, repurposing and combining structures. Technology adds our ability to anticipate what a combination might do, although we’re still constantly surprised by the results. So I’d see functional composition as a major source of cumulative complexity: each useful invention potentially becomes part of the vocabulary for making the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says inventions are built from existing capabilities and describes new arrangements of existing technologies becoming components for later inventions.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss independent inventors arriving at the same invention at the same time or prerequisite technologies becoming available.

r003.rationale: It mentions that interfaces matter, but does not say contingent design choices become locked in and shape later technologies that incorporate the invention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think functional composition is one of the fundamental ways technology evolves. You make something that does a particular job, and then that becomes a component in something else. The new thing doesn’t have to reinvent all the capabilities of its parts. It can build on them.

Software makes this especially explicit. You have functions that can call other functions, and you can build increasingly elaborate behaviors out of relatively simple pieces. But the same principle applies to physical technologies. A motor becomes part of a machine, and that machine becomes part of a larger system.

What’s interesting is that this makes the space of possibilities combinatorial. An invention doesn’t just add one more thing to the world; it potentially changes what you can make with everything that’s already there. Of course, the pieces have to fit together, and making them fit is often where the hard engineering happens.

So I’d see technological evolution less as a succession of isolated breakthroughs and more as a cumulative process of composition, where existing capabilities become the building blocks for new ones.

r001.rationale: The response says technologies become components in larger systems and that new inventions build on existing capabilities rather than reinventing them.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss independent inventors converging on the same invention when prerequisite technologies become available.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how contingent design choices become fixed and shape later technologies that incorporate the invention.
